>> On May 17, 2024 at 12:08 PM -0600, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>,
>> wrote:
>>
>> Shaun,
>>
>> Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in Project
>> Status.
>>
>> *Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after
>> this code finishes?*: There are always other options, like your loading
>> modal solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability
>> then the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time
>> to wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question
>> I would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent
>> experience?
>>
>> I'll reference some other ideas later on.
>>
>> *Why does it work better in Production?*: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a
>> factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in
>> Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development
>> that Mark setup, which is normal.
>>
>> I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult
>> Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
>>  <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
>> This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I
>> refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft
>> refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen
>> faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just
>> because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns
>> false and has no further payload to return.
>>
>> Breaking down the operation...
>>  1. The page loads all initial page elements
>>  2. Loading... is the default div element
>>  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via GraphQL
>> query
>>  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected
>> into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
>> I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
>>  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and
>> after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it
>> there is no change to the issue.
>>  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these
>> manage load states of various components; however, I have not found
>> anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
>> [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I
>> attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
>>
>> Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps
>> this question <https://v2.vuejs.org/lts/>. They say to ask 3 questions:
>>  1. Is the website stable and working well?
>>  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the
>> future?
>>  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by
>> upgrading?
>> You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least
>> speak to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck.
>> The further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how
>> to utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
>>  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the
>> documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using
>> v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into
>> later.
>>  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning
>> out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to
>> Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2
>> version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
>> Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the
>> website "will no longer receive updates, including security and browser
>> compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on
>> accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox
>> and Chromium based browsers.
>>
>> The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well
>> and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
>> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
>> I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin
>> so I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several
>> examples where Vue2 support is fading.
>>
>> Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible
>> plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man
>> power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run
>> upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
>>
>> Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably,
>> *but* there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and
>> simplify modals and loading. For instance:
>>  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>
>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/teleport.html>: a reliable way to
>> handle modals
>>  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely
>> Typescript and better supports this methodology.
>>  • Composition API
>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/composition-api-faq.html> (CAPI) - this
>> is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it
>> supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and
>> onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the
>> Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins
>> <https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables#vs-mixins>, the primary
>> logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily
>> implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2
>> solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions
>> for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the time needed
>> to fix accessibility and future issues.
>>
>> What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a
>> package called @vue/compat
>> <https://v3-migration.vuejs.org/migration-build> which essentially is a
>> transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue with
>> Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that bring the
>> code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can significantly
>> reduce the time to production for Vue3.
>>
>> These are the three basic parts to the migration:
>>  1. *Check Compatibility*: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify
>> any issues with the current setup.
>>  2. *Upgrade and Test*: Upgrade dependencies and test each one
>> incrementally to identify breaking changes.
>>  3. *Seek Alternatives*: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look
>> for actively maintained alternatives.
>> Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration,
>> this is a quick overview:
>>
>> *Direct Vue 2 Dependencies* 1. *vue*: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
>>  2. *vue-template-compiler*: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue
>> 3.
>> *Vue Ecosystem Packages* 1. *vue-loader*: Ensure use of the version
>> compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
>>  2. *eslint-plugin-vue*: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
>>  3. *@storybook/vue*: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or
>> remove.
>> *Vue Plugins and Libraries* 1. *vue-clickaway*: Check if there's a
>> version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
>>  2. *vue-gallery-slideshow*: Verify compatibility or look for an
>> alternative library.
>>  3. *vue-wait*: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
>>  4. *vuex*: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
>>  5. *vuex-persistedstate*: Check for a compatible version.
>>  6. *vuex-shared-mutations*: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or
>> find an alternative.
>> *Other Dependencies to Review* 1. *@storybook/addon-essentials,
>> @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core,
>> @storybook/core-common*: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
>>  2. *babel-loader*: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible
>> with other dependencies.
>>  3. *css-loader, style-loader*: Generally should work, but ensure
>> compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
>>  4. *ts-loader, typescript*: Ensure they are configured correctly for
>> Vue 3 and TypeScript.
>>  5. *tailwindcss and related plugins*: Check compatibility but they are
>> generally framework-agnostic.
>>  6. *axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone*: These should work as they
>> are not directly tied to Vue.
>>  7. *node*: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
>> *Be aware*: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has
>> said they have stopped supporting IE as well
>> <https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2022/06/15/internet-explorer-11-has-retired-and-is-officially-out-of-support-what-you-need-to-know/>.
>> So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
>>
>> *Bonus*: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite
>> <https://vitejs.dev>, which could simplify our local dev environment
>> issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works
>> very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have
>> CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in
>> setup, but the results should be the same.
>>
>> *Final Thoughts*in the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from
>> upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
>>
>> In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained
>> package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the
>> Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like
>> the ones we're running into for accessibility.
>>
>> I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have any
>> questions.
>>
>> Thanks for your help and diligence.
>>

> > > On May 17, 2024 at 12:08 PM -0600, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>, wrote:
> > > > Shaun,
> > > >
> > > > Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in Project Status.
> > > >
> > > > Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after this code finishes?: There are always other options, like your loading modal solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability then the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time to wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question I would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent experience?
> > > >
> > > > I'll reference some other ideas later on.
> > > >
> > > > Why does it work better in Production?: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development that Mark setup, which is normal.
> > > >
> > > > I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
> > > > <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>   <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
> > > > This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns false and has no further payload to return.
> > > >
> > > > Breaking down the operation...
> > > >  1. The page loads all initial page elements
> > > >  2. Loading... is the default div element
> > > >  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via GraphQL query
> > > >  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
> > > > I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
> > > >  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it there is no change to the issue.
> > > >  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these manage load states of various components; however, I have not found anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
> > > > [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
> > > >
> > > > Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps this question. They say to ask 3 questions:
> > > >  1. Is the website stable and working well?
> > > >  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the future?
> > > >  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by upgrading?
> > > > You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least speak to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck. The further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how to utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
> > > >  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into later.
> > > >  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2 version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
> > > > Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the website "will no longer receive updates, including security and browser compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox and Chromium based browsers.
> > > >
> > > > The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
> > > > <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
> > > > <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
> > > > I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin so I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several examples where Vue2 support is fading.
> > > >
> > > > Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
> > > >
> > > > Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably, but there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and simplify modals and loading. For instance:
> > > >  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>: a reliable way to handle modals
> > > >  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely Typescript and better supports this methodology.
> > > >  • Composition API (CAPI) - this is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins, the primary logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2 solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the time needed to fix accessibility and future issues.
> > > >
> > > > What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a package called @vue/compat which essentially is a transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue with Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that bring the code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can significantly reduce the time to production for Vue3.
> > > >
> > > > These are the three basic parts to the migration:
> > > >  1. Check Compatibility: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify any issues with the current setup.
> > > >  2. Upgrade and Test: Upgrade dependencies and test each one incrementally to identify breaking changes.
> > > >  3. Seek Alternatives: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look for actively maintained alternatives.
> > > > Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration, this is a quick overview:
> > > >
> > > > Direct Vue 2 Dependencies 1. vue: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
> > > >  2. vue-template-compiler: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue 3.
> > > > Vue Ecosystem Packages 1. vue-loader: Ensure use of the version compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
> > > >  2. eslint-plugin-vue: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
> > > >  3. @storybook/vue: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or remove.
> > > > Vue Plugins and Libraries 1. vue-clickaway: Check if there's a version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
> > > >  2. vue-gallery-slideshow: Verify compatibility or look for an alternative library.
> > > >  3. vue-wait: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
> > > >  4. vuex: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
> > > >  5. vuex-persistedstate: Check for a compatible version.
> > > >  6. vuex-shared-mutations: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
> > > > Other Dependencies to Review 1. @storybook/addon-essentials, @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core, @storybook/core-common: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
> > > >  2. babel-loader: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible with other dependencies.
> > > >  3. css-loader, style-loader: Generally should work, but ensure compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
> > > >  4. ts-loader, typescript: Ensure they are configured correctly for Vue 3 and TypeScript.
> > > >  5. tailwindcss and related plugins: Check compatibility but they are generally framework-agnostic.
> > > >  6. axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone: These should work as they are not directly tied to Vue.
> > > >  7. node: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
> > > > Be aware: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has said they have stopped supporting IE as well. So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
> > > >
> > > > Bonus: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite, which could simplify our local dev environment issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in setup, but the results should be the same.
> > > >
> > > > Final Thoughtsin the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
> > > >
> > > > In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like the ones we're running into for accessibility.
> > > >
> > > > I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have any questions.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for your help and diligence.

> On May 17, 2024 at 12:08 PM -0600, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>,
> wrote:
>
> Shaun,
>
> Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in Project
> Status.
>
> *Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after this
> code finishes?*: There are always other options, like your loading modal
> solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability then
> the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time to
> wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question I
> would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent experience?
>
> I'll reference some other ideas later on.
>
> *Why does it work better in Production?*: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a
> factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in
> Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development
> that Mark setup, which is normal.
>
> I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult
> Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
>  <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
> This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I
> refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft
> refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen
> faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just
> because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns
> false and has no further payload to return.
>
> Breaking down the operation...
>  1. The page loads all initial page elements
>  2. Loading... is the default div element
>  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via GraphQL
> query
>  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected
> into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
> I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
>  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and
> after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it
> there is no change to the issue.
>  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these
> manage load states of various components; however, I have not found
> anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
> [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I
> attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
>
> Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps
> this question <https://v2.vuejs.org/lts/>. They say to ask 3 questions:
>  1. Is the website stable and working well?
>  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the
> future?
>  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by
> upgrading?
> You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least speak
> to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck. The
> further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how to
> utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
>  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the
> documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using
> v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into
> later.
>  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning out
> since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to
> Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2
> version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
> Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the
> website "will no longer receive updates, including security and browser
> compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on
> accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox
> and Chromium based browsers.
>
> The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well
> and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
> I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin so
> I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several examples
> where Vue2 support is fading.
>
> Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible
> plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man
> power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run
> upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
>
> Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably,
> *but* there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and
> simplify modals and loading. For instance:
>  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>
> <https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/teleport.html>: a reliable way to
> handle modals
>  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely
> Typescript and better supports this methodology.
>  • Composition API
> <https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/composition-api-faq.html> (CAPI) - this
> is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it
> supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and
> onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the
> Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins
> <https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables#vs-mixins>, the primary
> logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily
> implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2
> solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions
> for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the time needed
> to fix accessibility and future issues.
>
> What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a
> package called @vue/compat
> <https://v3-migration.vuejs.org/migration-build> which essentially is a
> transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue with
> Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that bring the
> code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can significantly
> reduce the time to production for Vue3.
>
> These are the three basic parts to the migration:
>  1. *Check Compatibility*: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify
> any issues with the current setup.
>  2. *Upgrade and Test*: Upgrade dependencies and test each one
> incrementally to identify breaking changes.
>  3. *Seek Alternatives*: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look
> for actively maintained alternatives.
> Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration, this
> is a quick overview:
>
> *Direct Vue 2 Dependencies* 1. *vue*: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
>  2. *vue-template-compiler*: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue 3.
> *Vue Ecosystem Packages* 1. *vue-loader*: Ensure use of the version
> compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
>  2. *eslint-plugin-vue*: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
>  3. *@storybook/vue*: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or
> remove.
> *Vue Plugins and Libraries* 1. *vue-clickaway*: Check if there's a
> version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
>  2. *vue-gallery-slideshow*: Verify compatibility or look for an
> alternative library.
>  3. *vue-wait*: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
>  4. *vuex*: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
>  5. *vuex-persistedstate*: Check for a compatible version.
>  6. *vuex-shared-mutations*: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or find
> an alternative.
> *Other Dependencies to Review* 1. *@storybook/addon-essentials,
> @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core,
> @storybook/core-common*: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
>  2. *babel-loader*: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible with
> other dependencies.
>  3. *css-loader, style-loader*: Generally should work, but ensure
> compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
>  4. *ts-loader, typescript*: Ensure they are configured correctly for Vue
> 3 and TypeScript.
>  5. *tailwindcss and related plugins*: Check compatibility but they are
> generally framework-agnostic.
>  6. *axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone*: These should work as they
> are not directly tied to Vue.
>  7. *node*: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
> *Be aware*: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has
> said they have stopped supporting IE as well
> <https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2022/06/15/internet-explorer-11-has-retired-and-is-officially-out-of-support-what-you-need-to-know/>.
> So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
>
> *Bonus*: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite
> <https://vitejs.dev>, which could simplify our local dev environment
> issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works
> very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have
> CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in
> setup, but the results should be the same.
>
> *Final Thoughts*in the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from
> upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
>
> In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained
> package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the
> Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like
> the ones we're running into for accessibility.
>
> I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have any
> questions.
>
> Thanks for your help and diligence.
>

On May 17, 2024 at 12:08 PM -0600, Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>, wrote:
> Shaun,
>
> Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in Project Status.
>
> Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after this code finishes?: There are always other options, like your loading modal solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability then the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time to wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question I would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent experience?
>
> I'll reference some other ideas later on.
>
> Why does it work better in Production?: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development that Mark setup, which is normal.
>
> I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>   <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png>
> This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns false and has no further payload to return.
>
> Breaking down the operation...
>  1. The page loads all initial page elements
>  2. Loading... is the default div element
>  • the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via GraphQL query
>  3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.
> I have checked a couple of possibilities today:
>  • v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it there is no change to the issue.
>  • I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these manage load states of various components; however, I have not found anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.
> [ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]
>
> Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps this question. They say to ask 3 questions:
>  1. Is the website stable and working well?
>  2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the future?
>  3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by upgrading?
> You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least speak to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck. The further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how to utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:
>  1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into later.
>  2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2 version anymore - I'll reference this again later.
> Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the website "will no longer receive updates, including security and browser compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox and Chromium based browsers.
>
> The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png>
> <Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png>
> I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin so I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several examples where Vue2 support is fading.
>
> Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.
>
> Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably, but there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and simplify modals and loading. For instance:
>  • Vue3 introduced <Teleport>: a reliable way to handle modals
>  • A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely Typescript and better supports this methodology.
>  • Composition API (CAPI) - this is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins, the primary logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily implemented throughout.To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2 solution to these two pressing problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions for them. Being able to utilize these features will shorten the time needed to fix accessibility and future issues.
>
> What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a package called @vue/compat which essentially is a transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality to continue with Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning messages that bring the code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I think we can significantly reduce the time to production for Vue3.
>
> These are the three basic parts to the migration:
>  1. Check Compatibility: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify any issues with the current setup.
>  2. Upgrade and Test: Upgrade dependencies and test each one incrementally to identify breaking changes.
>  3. Seek Alternatives: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look for actively maintained alternatives.
> Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration, this is a quick overview:
>
> Direct Vue 2 Dependencies 1. vue: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
>  2. vue-template-compiler: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue 3.
> Vue Ecosystem Packages 1. vue-loader: Ensure use of the version compatible with Vue 3, which would be vue-loader@next.
>  2. eslint-plugin-vue: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
>  3. @storybook/vue: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or remove.
> Vue Plugins and Libraries 1. vue-clickaway: Check if there's a version compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
>  2. vue-gallery-slideshow: Verify compatibility or look for an alternative library.
>  3. vue-wait: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
>  4. vuex: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
>  5. vuex-persistedstate: Check for a compatible version.
>  6. vuex-shared-mutations: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or find an alternative.
> Other Dependencies to Review 1. @storybook/addon-essentials, @storybook/addons, @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core, @storybook/core-common: Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
>  2. babel-loader: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible with other dependencies.
>  3. css-loader, style-loader: Generally should work, but ensure compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
>  4. ts-loader, typescript: Ensure they are configured correctly for Vue 3 and TypeScript.
>  5. tailwindcss and related plugins: Check compatibility but they are generally framework-agnostic.
>  6. axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone: These should work as they are not directly tied to Vue.
>  7. node: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.
> Be aware: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has said they have stopped supporting IE as well. So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.
>
> Bonus: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite, which could simplify our local dev environment issue and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works very well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have CraftCMS, Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in setup, but the results should be the same.
>
> Final Thoughtsin the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from upgrading I think will be worth the extra time and work now.
>
> In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like the ones we're running into for accessibility.
>
> I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have any questions.
>
> Thanks for your help and diligence.
>

==== EMAIL 312 ====
Date: Fri, 17 May 2024 12:07:48 -0600
From: Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>
To:   Shaun Cooney <shaun@monumentgraphics.com>
Subject: Re: Aspen Rec - Project Status

Shaun,

Regarding Vue2 to Vue3 migration, I figure this one should go in Project
Status.

*Do we have any other options to prevent the close of the menus after this
code finishes?*: There are always other options, like your loading modal
solution; however, if our primary goal is accessibility and usability then
the loading modal will increase a user pain-point, i.e. increased time to
wait before they can access the information on the page. So the question I
would ask is: what will give users the fastest, most consistent experience?

I'll reference some other ideas later on.

*Why does it work better in Production?*: "Dev mode" in Servd might be a
factor, which introduces additional operations that don't run in
Production. There are also configurations enabled specific to development
that Mark setup, which is normal.

I ran Lighthouse on the dev environment and production pages for "Adult
Hockey", these were the results (dev on left | production on right):
[image: Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-09-12 Lighthouse Report
Viewer.png]   [image:
Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 12-11-55 Lighthouse Report Viewer.png]
This test at least doesn't show much difference in performance and if I
refresh in production and hover over a menu to open the dropdown the soft
refresh does still occur and resets the dropdown. It does seem to happen
faster in production so I see what you mean there, but this is likely just
because there's nothing to get. In other words, it immediately returns
false and has no further payload to return.

Breaking down the operation...

   1. The page loads all initial page elements
   2. Loading... is the default div element
      - the code checks CraftCMS if there is a closure to display via
      GraphQL query
   3. The closure element (if true) or an empty div (if false) is injected
   into the DOM tree, which causes the soft reload.

I have checked a couple of possibilities today:

   - v-show instead of v-if because v-show is present in the DOM before and
   after and so shouldn't have the soft refresh; however, upon testing it
   there is no change to the issue.
   - I reviewed the getters, store, mutations and actions JS files - these
   manage load states of various components; however, I have not found
   anything to be improved or optimized for this use case.

[ Side note: I discovered a file called lazy-load-component which I
attempted to use to fix the modal problem, but no success. ]

Answering the question "is it necessary?": Vue has an article that helps
this question <https://v2.vuejs.org/lts/>. They say to ask 3 questions:

   1. Is the website stable and working well?
   2. Does the website expect continued new feature development into the
   future?
   3. Is there a pain-point or bottleneck that can only be solved by
   upgrading?

You would be able to answer the first two better, but I can at least speak
to the third: accessibility is likely that pain-point / bottleneck. The
further I dig into this the more I'm finding conflicting advice on how to
utilize Vue, even for Vue 2, which seems to stem from two reasons:

   1.  Vue 2.7 included several concepts from Vue 3 and so some of the
   documentation and blogs use 2.7 syntax and simply say Vue2. Aspen is using
   v2.5.17 and so doesn't have access to several features, which I'll go into
   later.
   2. EOL occurred in December of last year, but it's been transitioning
   out since 2020. This problem is compounded with plugins related to
   Vue. @storybook plugin for instance doesn't even have code for any Vue2
   version anymore - I'll reference this again later.

Could we kick the can down the road? We could; however, in Vue2 the website
"will no longer receive updates, including security and browser
compatibility fixes", which is something I've noted while working on
accessibility - e.g. different accessibility experiences on Safari, Firefox
and Chromium based browsers.

The dependencies associated with Vue will no longer be supported as well
and some have entirely removed their packages already, like this:
[image: Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.46.23 AM.png]
[image: Screenshot 2024-05-16 at 10.43.23 AM.png]
I actually can't find any Aspen code that utilizes the storybook plugin so
I don't see any reason for it to be here, but it's one of several examples
where Vue2 support is fading.

Because of this Vue recommends building your own in-house Vue2 compatible
plugins and supporting them yourself. This will take considerably more man
power and time than I think Aspen wants to put into it. So in the long run
upgrading will cost Aspen less time and money.

Could we get the modal and loading to work without upgrading? Probably,
*but* there are built-in parts of Vue3 that specifically enhance and
simplify modals and loading. For instance:

   - Vue3 introduced <Teleport>
   <https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/teleport.html>: a reliable way to
   handle modals
   - A large portion of the Aspen code relies on "types" - Vue3 is entirely
   Typescript and better supports this methodology.
   - Composition API
   <https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/composition-api-faq.html>(CAPI) - this
   is the single largest advantage to Vue3 for the modals & loading because it
   supports Reactivity APIs and Lifecycle Hooks - things like ref() and
   onMounted(), which we are using older versions of utilizing mixins and the
   Options API. CAPI, however, solves all the drawbacks of mixins
   <https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables#vs-mixins>, the primary
   logic reuse mechanism for Options API - which is what Mark primarily
   implemented throughout.

To say it another way, I don't have a Vue2 solution to these two pressing
problems yet, but I do have Vue3 solutions for them. Being able to utilize
these features will shorten the time needed to fix accessibility and future
issues.

What exactly will the migration entail? I discovered that Vue has a package
called @vue/compat <https://v3-migration.vuejs.org/migration-build> which
essentially is a transition between Vue2 and 3 which allows functionality
to continue with Vue2 syntax while sorting out the error and warning
messages that bring the code up to Vue3 syntax compliance. Using this, I
think we can significantly reduce the time to production for Vue3.

These are the three basic parts to the migration:

   1. *Check Compatibility*: Use the Vue 3 compatibility build to identify
   any issues with the current setup.
   2. *Upgrade and Test*: Upgrade dependencies and test each one
   incrementally to identify breaking changes.
   3. *Seek Alternatives*: If a package is not compatible with Vue 3, look
   for actively maintained alternatives.

Updating the packages and dependencies is essential to the migration, this
is a quick overview:


*Direct Vue 2 Dependencies*

   1. *vue*: update to vue@next for Vue 3.
   2. *vue-template-compiler*: Replace this with @vue/compiler-sfc in Vue 3.


*Vue Ecosystem Packages*

   1. *vue-loader*: Ensure use of the version compatible with Vue 3, which
   would be vue-loader@next.
   2. *eslint-plugin-vue*: Update to a version that supports Vue 3.
   3. *@storybook/vue*: Update to use the version compatible with Vue 3 or
   remove.


*Vue Plugins and Libraries*

   1. *vue-clickaway*: Check if there's a version compatible with Vue 3 or
   find an alternative.
   2. *vue-gallery-slideshow*: Verify compatibility or look for an
   alternative library.
   3. *vue-wait*: Check for Vue 3 support or find an alternative.
   4. *vuex*: Upgrade to Vuex 4, which is designed for Vue 3.
   5. *vuex-persistedstate*: Check for a compatible version.
   6. *vuex-shared-mutations*: Verify if it's compatible with Vue 3 or find
   an alternative.


*Other Dependencies to Review*

   1. *@storybook/addon-essentials, @storybook/addons,
   @storybook/builder-webpack5, @storybook/core, @storybook/core-common*:
   Update to Vue 3 compatible versions or remove.
   2. *babel-loader*: Should work as is, but make sure it's compatible with
   other dependencies.
   3. *css-loader, style-loader*: Generally should work, but ensure
   compatibility with Vue 3 setup.
   4. *ts-loader, typescript*: Ensure they are configured correctly for Vue
   3 and TypeScript.
   5. *tailwindcss and related plugins*: Check compatibility but they are
   generally framework-agnostic.
   6. *axios, core-js, moment, moment-timezone*: These should work as they
   are not directly tied to Vue.
   7. *node*: Update to v20 so that Vuex will work.

*Be aware*: Vue3 does not support IE11 at all; however, Microsoft has said
they have stopped supporting IE as well
<https://blogs.windows.com/windowsexperience/2022/06/15/internet-explorer-11-has-retired-and-is-officially-out-of-support-what-you-need-to-know/>.
So I think this is fairly standard now - just a heads up.

*Bonus*: there is a possible bonus to Vue3 which is usage of Vite
<https://vitejs.dev>, which could simplify our local dev environment issue
and its sole purpose is to speed up front-end operations. It works very
well in the vue-project I built, but of course that doesn't have CraftCMS,
Docker or a database utilized so there will be some variances in setup, but
the results should be the same.

*Final Thoughts*
in the long run, the time and money saved for Aspen from upgrading I think
will be worth the extra time and work now.

In summary, Vue3 will take less time to maintain, has actively maintained
package options, which means less bugs, and is actively supported by the
Vue community, which means easier to find solutions when bugs arise - like
the ones we're running into for accessibility.

I've tried to be as thorough as possible but let me know if you have any
questions.

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > 1. > > > > > > > CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't exist.
> > > > > > >     • It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g., language settings, UI settings).
> > > > > > >     • Since the table is missing, the query fails, causing the error you see.
> > > > > > > 2. > > > > > > > The table was probably created manually at some point but is not included in active migrations.
> > > > > > >     • If it were a CraftCMS core table, it would have been recreated automatically.
> > > > > > >     • Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a custom migration or a plugin that is no longer active.

drop-ins section of the code allowing for the null value so it should be a
quick patch.

> Basically, what's going on is that it's looking for a table called
> userpreferences and can't find it.
>
> The only codebase reference to userpreferences is in *seed_db.sql*, this
> means:
>
>    - The userpreferences table *was never created* in the active
>    database, or
>    - It was *dropped at some point* and not recreated.
>
> *What This Means for the Error*
>
>    1.
>
>    *CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't
>    exist.*
>    - It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g.,
>       language settings, UI settings).
>       - Since the table is missing, the query *fails*, causing the error
>       you see.
>    2.
>
>    *The table was probably created manually at some point but is not
>    included in active migrations.*
>    - If it were a *CraftCMS core table*, it would have been recreated
>       automatically.
>       - Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a *custom
>       migration or a plugin* that is no longer active.
>
> My inclination would be that it's an issue with one of these plugins:
>
>    - SEOmatic
>    - Redactor
>    - Formie
>
> If I had to guess, I'd bet on Redactor as the offending plugin.

2025-01-31 18:58:22 [web.WARNING] [application] Request context:

Basically, what's going on is that it's looking for a table called
userpreferences and can't find it.

The only codebase reference to userpreferences is in *seed_db.sql*, this
means:

   - The userpreferences table *was never created* in the active database,
   or
   - It was *dropped at some point* and not recreated.

*What This Means for the Error*

   1.

   *CraftCMS is trying to query a table (userpreferences) that doesn't
   exist.*
   - It is likely expecting this table to store user preferences (e.g.,
      language settings, UI settings).
      - Since the table is missing, the query *fails*, causing the error
      you see.
   2.

   *The table was probably created manually at some point but is not
   included in active migrations.*
   - If it were a *CraftCMS core table*, it would have been recreated
      automatically.
      - Since it's only in seed_db.sql, it might have been part of a *custom
      migration or a plugin* that is no longer active.

My inclination would be that it's an issue with one of these plugins:

   - SEOmatic
   - Redactor
   - Formie

If I had to guess, I'd bet on Redactor as the offending plugin.

The good news is that this should resolve with the package updates we have
planned.

Do you feel like this is pressing enough to need an immediate response or
will it be okay to resolve as I get there in the next month?

Hi Eric,

Thanks for looking into it.

To see the error, you’ll need to go to the Curling record within the activities collection (not the drop-in curling record under classes/events). Within the activity entry, there’s a drop-in tab with the old drop-in item de-activated. Re-activate that and I think the error should re-appear. However, due to caching, it may not show for you in your browser. To force everything to rebuild, here’s what I did:

1. Disable the caching in production in Servd (just a toggle switch in the settings); re-sync.
2. Turn on the drop-in record within the curling activity.
3. Use the cache-clearing tools in Craft Utilities.
4. Clear your browser cache by completely deleting all cookies and data for aspenrecreation.com.
5. Refresh page.
6. Check Servd error logs.

With any luck, you should see that the calendar loading stalls on the front end, and a PHP error shows in the Servd logs.

Apologies for not being clearer with that in my email last night.

We’re headed off to a family reunion today through Monday. I’ll keep an eye on this thread and try my best to respond if you have any additional questions.

If you wouldn’t mind, please be sure to set any entries and Servd settings back when you’ve concluded your investigation.

Thanks!

From: Eric Phifer <eric@ericphiferllc.com>

Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

On the other issues:

   - The news filters have been notoriously finicky from page to page. I've
   sorted it out now--the "showNews" logic just needed to be tweaked a bit.
   - In terms of the slow load times, I've been seeing the same thing and
   this is last on my list to test and optimize after everything else is in
   place. Part of this will be fixing the placeholders which aren't resolving
   currently and you're right that production should improve it some.
   - Forestry page, the spacing and fonts have changed how they work from
   1.9:
      - *v1.9 uses fixed design tokens defined
      in tailwind.config.js (discrete spacing scale; static text sizes). v4
      switches to CSS variables and formulas — spacing becomes “any integer
      × --spacing,” and text sizes/line-heights come from --text-*variables —
      while prose works the same but plugs into the new variable system.*
      - For instance, the old system
         - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
           <!-- mt-8 = 2rem (32px), p-4 = 1rem (16px) -->
         - The new system:
         - <div class="mt-8 p-4">
           <!-- mt-8 = calc(var(--spacing) * 8)
                p-4 = calc(var(--spacing) * 4) -->
         - I've been working on the base styling and I think I have things
      restored--there may still be some outliers. I removed the spacing
      definitions in app.pcss @theme section, which was a carryover from the
      tailwind.config.js v1.9 but seems to be interfering with the styling we
      want now.
   - The accessibility checker issues:
      - *Four landmark issues*:
         - navigation--top.vue has the <div class="flex-grow">
         - navigation-item--secondary.twig has the <span> Activity Calendar
         </span>
         - To fix this accessibility issue I added a <nav> as a parent
         element to main navigation, main navigation items and
"utility navigation
         items" for the secondary nav items which are all labelled now with
         aria-label
      - *Modal Accessible Name*:
         - modal--main.vue had this code and I added an aria-label fallback
         with a dynamic switch for each modal type and passed the ID
down to the
         component children which should ensure consistency for Screen Readers.
      - *Role Usage on Nav--Items*: the code referenced is in
      navigation--items.vue and the problem has to do with the menu role usage.
      The menu role shouldn't be necessary here since we're using a
semantic nav
      element with a descriptive aria-label so I just removed the
roles and this
      should be clean now.

All that's left on my list now is the performance issues with slow load
times and placeholder usage.

>>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used
>>>>    focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use
>>>>    the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
>>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
>>>>
>>>> Other notes:
>>>>
>>>>    1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font
>>>>    size was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I
>>>>    see the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
>>>>    gray-600.
>>>>    2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is
>>>>    now fixed.
>>>>    3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm
>>>>    going through but using the predefined sizes--e.g. outline-thick, text-sm,
>>>>    etc.--don't seem to be exactly right so this is just a fine-tuning note
>>>>    that shouldn't affect accessibility.
>>>>
>>>> Just pushed the corrections to dev so that should be updated within a
>>>> few minutes

>>>> Okay, thank you again for the feedback.

>>>> There was a lingering "redactor" reference in the project.yaml file
>>>> that I corrected. Dev mostly reflects local now--the dev database is
>>>> slightly different from local but this isn't crucial since the database and
>>>> assets are going to update to production anyway. So it's safe now to
>>>> continue with your points:
>>>>
>>>>    1. Got it. That color is corrected.
>>>>    2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on
>>>>    this last--now that is.
>>>>    3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
>>>>    4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so
>>>>    thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple
>>>>    naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was
>>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used
>>>>    focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use
>>>>    the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
>>>>    6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
>>>>    reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
>>>>
>>>> Other notes:
>>>>
>>>>    1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font
>>>>    size was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I
>>>>    see the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
>>>>    gray-600.
>>>>    2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is
>>>>    now fixed.
>>>>    3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm
>>>>    going through but using the predefined sizes--e.g. outline-thick, text-sm,
>>>>    etc.--don't seem to be exactly right so this is just a fine-tuning note
>>>>    that shouldn't affect accessibility.

The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.

>>>    outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than
>>>    swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the
>>>    repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances
>>>    which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a
>>>    bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to
>>>    "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if
>>>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.
>>>    5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-*
>>>    as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-*
>>>    directly and the focus is implied.

> > > > > 4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.
> > > > > 5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.

Dev mostly reflects local now--the dev database is slightly different from local but this isn't crucial since the database and assets are going to update to production anyway. So it's safe now to continue with your points:
> >
> > 1. Got it. That color is corrected.
> > 2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on this last--now that is.
> > 3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
> > 4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of !important to override variables for particular instances which would occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner. To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a different naming convention you prefer.
> > 5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-* directly and the focus is implied.
> > 6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.
> >
> > Other notes:
> >
> > 1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font size was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I see the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to gray-600.
> > 2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is now fixed.
> > 3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm going through but using the predefined sizes--e.g. outline-thick, text-sm, etc.--don't seem to be exactly right so this is just a fine-tuning note that shouldn't affect accessibility.

>    you have a different naming convention you prefer.

>    directly and the focus is implied.

Okay, thank you again for the feedback.

There was a lingering "redactor" reference in the project.yaml file that I
corrected. Dev mostly reflects local now--the dev database is slightly
different from local but this isn't crucial since the database and assets
are going to update to production anyway. So it's safe now to continue with
your points:

   1. Got it. That color is corrected.
   2. This one has some potential to be meddlesome so I'm working on this
   last--now that is.
   3. This was corrected by removing the stray redactor reference.
   4. I believe this one was on a checklist from a few months ago so thanks
   for bringing it up again. The reason for the mismatch is a simple naming
   convention. The neutral outline color in the old code was outline-gray and
   in the new code we redefine the color variable rather than swap them out to
   fit each outline case. This was in part to avoid the repeated use of
   !important to override variables for particular instances which would
   occasionally result in unforeseen behavior--making the code a bit cleaner.
   To fix it, I'll just change the naming convention to "outline-base" to
   avoid confusion. This is a quick and easy change too if you have a
   different naming convention you prefer.
   5. Thanks for noting this. Before the update we used focus:outline-* as
   inline css; however, with the new Tailwind set up we use the outline-*
   directly and the focus is implied.
   6. Gotcha. Yeah, this was in the aspect-ratio troubleshooting. I
   reintroduced xl:h-full to the <picture> element and that fixed it.

Other notes:

   1. I came across one other mismatch with the navigation: the font size
   was a touch smaller so I set it to initial and that has fixed it and I see
   the color is black in dev but gray-600 in production so I set that to
   gray-600.
   2. I also came across a scroll issue on the class modal, which is now
   fixed.
   3. I started working on the font-size differences I see as I'm going
   through but using the predefined sizes--e.g. outline-thick, text-sm,
   etc.--don't seem to be exactly right so this is just a fine-tuning note
   that shouldn't affect accessibility.

Just pushed the corrections to dev so that should be updated within a few
minutes

Subject: Re: Vue/Tailwind Updates

Hi Eric,

Thanks for the video. I’m sorry you had to rebuild so much of the code manually.

Overall, this is looking much better. There are still some minor visual differences I’ll note below. The more important items to address would be:

1. The focus outline color for the social icons in the footer needs to match the icon hover color. It currently does not have enough contrast. I believe that should be "--outline-black” –› #181919.
2. I do believe the arrow issues will need to be corrected on mobile, as that’ll come up in the validation.
3. The callout text in the gray box below the slider is missing. This appears tied to a redactor field that wasn’t updated. You can find that text field under ‘Entries › Singles › Homepage’.

Other, less pressing differences I noticed:

3. The menu items seem to be using a different color for the focus outline. The current one meets contrast, so this doesn’t present an accessibility issue, but it may cause a little confusion in the code. Production uses a value of #27871c defined via a CSS rule. Dev uses a value of #0f5d22, which is a dark green. In and of itself, that’s fine. The confusing part is that the value comes from "--outline-gray”, so I’m not sure why that value is outputting a green color instead of gray.

4. The focus outlines for the news filters, news items, and blog posts is gray instead of blue. Both meet contrast, so it’s not an accessibility issue, just a minor one I noticed.

5. There’s a small white gap below the thumbnail of news items. Not an accessibility issue, just some extra spacing that appears to have been introduced somewhere down the line that makes those seem a bit untidy.


I realize the last three are very minor and you’ve spent tons of time already, so if things are currently set up for me to make edits to the code, push to GitHub, and rebuild the bundle in Serv’d as we did before, I can plan on making those changes. Otherwise, if we need to revisit that process of how I make changes, please let me know.

Thanks,

Hey Shaun,

Thanks for the feedback.

That's not surprising. I had to restructure and rewrite the vast majority
of the front end code since Tailwind 4 is so different from 1.9, Pinia
storage is very different from Vuex and Vue3 has syntactic changes from
Vue2, plus the required update from Node 16 to Node 20.18. Since very
little of the original code has actually survived this update it's amazing
that I've made it look so close. 🤣

I'm sending a video with the side by side comparison after I've made a
couple of updates. Let me know if you're seeing the same things.
 aspen-side-by-side.mp4

Updating you on the project, I am making progress; I figured out the

page visited, when I fix this, the activity pages stop filtering and show
all events.

Quick question with that: do you want the events for each week to show for
the full week as they currently do in production or do you want the events
to be removed by day? (e.g. on a Wednesday, events for Sunday, Monday,
Tuesday won't show.) I have it set to the latter currently--an
unintentional change while figuring out the filtering--but I can easily
switch it back. Just wanted to check which functionality works better for
Aspen.

Once I sort out the filters, the calendar should be 100%--that's what I'm
looking to wrap up this week. I'm going through our past checklists and I'm
about 60% through them.

I still have an eye to releasing a functional version as soon as possible.

I do have some improvements I haven't pushed to dev yet so let me know if
you need to see the latest.

On a side note, Joseph Center is trying to raise funds to keep their doors
open so I'm helping with the technology and marketing aspects of that.
Every other spare moment I have I'm putting toward wrapping up Aspen--I
know we're all ready for it to be done and I'm using every resource I have
available to make that happen this month.

>

>

>    - Slideout arrow should rotate 180º
>
> *Calendar*:
>
>
>    - Tabbable items on the left side of an open modal have the focus

>    - Location has an empty tabbable item in the open modal

>
>
>    - When Multiple Tabs are active, "Enter" does not switch the tab
>    content
>
> *Modal*:
>
>
>    - Tabbing is not trapped
>
> *Dynamically Loaded Content*:
>
>
>    - "Soft Refresh" closes navigation
>
> So, to round out our list, here are the mobile-related items I found:
>
> *NAVIGATION*
> 25) Mobile nav format on expanded Youth Activites & Adult Activities
> doesn’t match production. The updates cause the “Adult Activities” to slide
> over and float to the left of the expanded menu on mobile.
> 26) Hover and focus states do match between dev and production on mobile
> 27) [Referencing from the original June 13, 2024 issue]: When zoomed in,
> mouseout should not close the slideout (grandchild items)
> 28) [Referencing from the original June 13, 2024 issue]: Arrows for the
> expanded Youth or Adult Activity submenus should change direction based on
> whether they are open or closed.
> 29) There is a missing space between the bold and regular weight words at
> the top level of the nav, causing it to read “Parkstrails”, “moreinfo”, etc.
>
> *CALENDAR*
> 29) On mobile, the width of the day header cells doesn’t match the width
> of the event columns, causing them to not match up, making it difficuly to
> tell which events belong with which day of the week.
> 30) On narrower devices, if the calendar needs to scroll hozizontally, the
> day of the week doesn’t scroll over with the content, resulting in
> mismatched days of the week to the corresponding events below.
> 31) Also on narrower devices, the controls to advance weeks split apart
> and are arranged awkwardly. This is something that probably existed before,
> but if there’s a way to quickly fix it, we probably should. I can take over
> this one if you’d like to draw the line on these types of requests.

> To prepare, I’ve done a deeper dive comparing the two sites and came up
> with the following list. I’ve assigned a star rating indicating relative
> priority. The more asterisks before an item, the more important it is from
> an operating/accessibility standpoint. Hopefully, most of these are
> relatively minor:
>
>
> *NATURAL RESOURCES & FORESTRY PAGES*
> 1) ***Template errors - cannot view pages
>
> *NAVIGATION*
> 2) **Top three items in black text are missing their previous focus states
> 3) **Elements (input, search, close) within search are missing the
> previous focus states
> 4) Search results are missing thumbnail images (possibly due to this being
> a subdomain?)
>
> *MODALS*
> 5) *If I visit the homepage, close the modal, then visit another page and
> return to the homepage, the modal loads in the last position I was in
> (i.e., displays an individual item, rather than the entire list). Can we
> set this to “forget” the user’s last interaction and load it fresh each
> time? Also curious if there’s any way to limit loading this to once per
> user session? (Only need info regarding this last query, please don’t make
> a change yet).
> 6) **When navigating to view more info about an item or "go back" within
> the modals, the focus isn't initially set, and my screen reader reads as
> though it's on a new page, rather than a changed modal on the same page.
> 7) *If the page is refreshed while a modal is open, the focus state seems
> to highlight a random area from the last state the modal was at and the
> screen reader will read out content that doesn’t match what’s on screen.
> 8) All text is currently centered. Can we set this back to left-aligned as
> before?
>
> *FOOTER*
> 9) **Subscribe popup –› Focus states and error styles are missing when
> using keyboard.
>
> *CALENDARS*
> 10) ***If using keyboard to open an event modal, the focus correctly goes
> to the close button. However, if the Enter key is used to close the modal,
> it immediately reopens it and forms a never-ending loop that can't be
> escaped unless the user knows to use the space key.
> 11) **Focus states for expanded calendar filters are missing their
> previous focus states
> 12) “Filter Calendar” heading is showing on non-filterable calendars
> (i.e., on activity or facility pages). There’s a chance this may have been
> my doing since it exists on both sites, so if you feel this is out of
> scope, please let me know.
>
> *CONTENT CONTAINERS*
> 13) All pages with <div class=“container”> are narrower than before. Can
> we adjust the width to match?
> 14) Homepage: News items are stretching too wide. Looks like the div with
> the container class is missing from this section.
>
> *BLUE CALLOUTS (Sitewide)*
> 15) *Button focus states need to be restored for contrast.
>
> *HERO SLIDERS*
> 16) **Slide controls are missing their previous focus states
> 17) Load time for initial image seems very slow (might be due to
> environment caching?)
> 18) *Hero images are shorter on homepage & Parks Dept. Landing page; Hero
> on Parks landing page is exceedingly tall (
> https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/parks-trails/aspen-area-parks).
>
> *STATUS UPDATES*
> 19) **Title shifts from stacked on top to floating left when opened (I
> believe this is a bug from our first round of work).
>
> *NEWS ITEMS*
> 20) *Screen readers need to provide notification when content changes via
> filters
>
> *PHOTO GALLERIES*
> 21) **not keyboard operable (
> https://dev.aspenrecreation.com/activities/full-day-camp/youth)
>
> *ACTIVITY PAGES*
> 22) Is there an easy way to allow keyboard users to skip over the activity
> tables? BeAccessible was suggesting we do this.
>
> ------------------------------
>
> *OTHER MINOR DIFFERENCES*
> 23) The focus states (text color changes and outline colors/styles) for
> news filter controls, passes, attractions (Rec Centers), news items,
